Row.Text: Before the Roman conquest, much of northern Europe was inhabited by a people the Greeks and Romans recognized as a separate cultural group. It is from the Greeks that we get the name “Keltoi” (the Celts), and from the Romans the name “Galli” (the Gauls). These names both come from a proto-Celtic origin and would have referred to the same people – our modern use of "Gaul" to refer only to the area of modern France is a reflection of the lines of the later Roman Empire. In truth, the Gauls/Celts lived across the continent, from Iberia to the Balkans, and from northern Italy to the British Isles. Modern scholars group these various peoples together as one group based on a shared language and some shared cultural practices, but the indigenous people of Gaul never referred to themselves as Gauls, but rather as their various tribal names (Aedui, Arverni, Remi, etc.).

The story of the Gauls begins in the late Bronze Age as what is known as the Hallstatt culture. This was the predominant proto-Celtic speaking culture throughout Europe up to the sixth century BCE. There is almost no writing from this period, but several archaeological sites provide a wealth of artifacts showing advanced metalworking, trade, and a broad settlement pattern of villages and farms. The largest of these were located on hilltops and often included metal workshops. As the population began to urbanize and many sites became abandoned, the culture transitioned into what we now call La Tène, commonly known as Celtic, in the sixth century BCE.

Throughout the early La Tène period of the sixth through the fourth centuries, the culture spread across Europe, supplanting Hallstatt over time. Significant cultural interchange occurred across southern Gaul, following the trade lines from the Mediterranean and up through the riverways. During this period as well, the wine trade became significant and the export of metalworks from Gaul and import of pottery from Greece reached its height. We have very little written evidence from the Gauls themselves because Gallic histories and stories were kept orally by the druids (the lorekeepers, priests, and civic adjudicators of the tribes), but in this period of intercultural influence, Gauls adapted some writing practices from their neighbors. They created combined scripts from the various languages to which they were exposed, resulting in the Gallo-Roman, Gallo-Greek, and Gallo-Etruscan inscriptions we have today, predominantly in the form of devotions to various deities. This period of growth and cultural fecundity lasted about two hundred years until the pressures of expansion necessitated change.

By the fourth century, the Gauls' population expanded into areas bordering the Etruscans and Romans in what is now northern Italy. Though these groups had previous peaceful contact via trade, war broke out, both between Gauls and these civilizations as well as between different Gallic tribes, as the need for resources and land grew with the population. In 387 BCE, the Gauls sacked Rome under the leadership of Brennus, chieftain of the Senones, a Gallic tribe, establishing their status as the primary threat to Rome at that time. Skirmishes over the next decades in Italy resulted in a peace between Gaul and Rome that lasted for a few decades. Though the sack of Rome had no lasting negative consequences for Rome's power, it had a profound psychological effect, leading Romans to consider Gauls fearsome for centuries.

Throughout the third century, Gallic tribes allied with Rome's enemies (Carthage, the Etruscans, and others) to combat Roman expansion. Wins were traded, but by the start of the second century, Rome had occupied northern Italy (Cisalpine Gaul), defeated Carthage, and now looked ahead to Gallic lands beyond the Alps. It is during this period that we see the rise of the oppida, as Caesar named them, an expansion of the older hillforts to include additional portions of the settlement within a walled enclosure. The walls were made of both stone and wood, the wooden beams providing the internal structure while the stone provided an additional layer of resilience. So strong were these walls that Julius Caesar commented positively on their ingenuity in his writings.

By the late first century BCE, Gaul’s internal conflicts provided ample opportunity for Roman intervention. When northern tribes threatened the southern Gallic commerce centers, Rome came to their aid, but not with the intent of defending their independence. Rather, Rome used this opportunity for its own expansion, fully annexing Transalpine Gaul (modern Provence) in 121 BCE. In 113, the Cimbrian War broke out as the Cimbri and other Gallo-Germanic groups tried to migrate into new lands. They successfully defeated Rome in a series of battles, but were slow in their advance, allowing the Romans to recover. In 101, the Cimbri moved south through the Alps, but the superior Roman forces proved victorious. The Cimbri were decimated, their leaders killed, their women and children choosing suicide over slavery.

From Provence, Rome had a base to advance further military actions, and it had an economic hold over the ports along the Mediterranean as well as the riverways leading north. From here, Julius Caesar decided to move north and conquer the rest of Gaul, nominally due to the migration of various Gallic tribes, but more likely due to his career ambitions and rising debts. Initially, Gallic tribes put up a strong fight, even defeating Caesar, yet by 56 BCE, Julius had turned the tables and defeated the Veneti (a tribe of seafarers from modern Brittany), taking much of northwestern Gaul. The Gauls reacted strongly. For the first time, a Gallic chieftain, Vercingetorix, began uniting the tribes in an effort to hold their land against the Roman invaders. Yet, despite a series of Gallic victories, the Romans eventually were victorious. Caesar went home to deal with Rome's civil wars, but Gaul would never reclaim her independence. Revolts continued into the first century AD, but the Roman conquest of Gaul was final.

The Roman conquest severely impacted the Gallic population. It is estimated that 1 in 12 Gauls were killed and the same number enslaved. Some tribes were completely eliminated and entire cities slaughtered. As Gaul settled disquietly into a Roman province, old oppida became Roman cities, and eventually Gauls were granted Roman citizenship in 212 CE. The hybridized Gallo-Roman language and culture further developed, eventually mixing with Frankish and other cultures in the urban centers of the Loire Valley during the early medieval period. Even today, Gallic culture remains an element of identity in modern France.

A nemeton was a Celtic sanctuary situated near a natural space, often a grove or a lake, either located outside but near a settlement or within as part of the enclosed area. Gallic religion highly valued the natural world and many of its deities were aspects of nature. One Gallic practice involved depositing valuable objects in lakes as offerings to their gods, a custom which has left us important archaeological evidence such as at the site of La Tène. The word “nemeton” is derived from the Gallic goddess Nemetona, who was worshipped in northern Gaul, Germany, and into the British Isles.

Though Roman writers described the groves as fearful places of wicked magic, they were more likely simply gathering places for both ritual and civic processes. Druids of different tribes are described as meeting together in a kind of council at a nemeton in a central location. Nemeta are known to have existed throughout Celtic Europe, as far east as Anatolia and north into the British Isles. Today, many place names, especially in France, retain references to the word, and in Brittany, one can visit the Névet Forest, once a Gallic nemeton.

A central part of Gallic settlements was the metalsmithing workshop, or goben, the Gallic word for a blacksmith. Gallic artisans were well-known for their craftsmanship and creativity, and within Gallic society, they were highly valued, holding a high place in the social hierarchy. Using metals like iron, bronze, and gold, Gallic smiths created common items used by the general population, both domestic and military, as well as ornate works of art, many of which have been found in graves and in lakes like at La Tène. In addition, metalworking was a significant element of the Gallic economy, forming the foundation of trade both between Gallic tribes and externally with other cultural groups. Gauls would export their craftsmanship in exchange for items like Greek pottery and Etruscan ceramics.

During the Halstatt and early La Tène periods, the goben would typically be placed on the hilltop in the center of the settlement as part of the enclosure. In the late La Tène period and after, workshops moved to the outskirts as settlements shifted their use of space and expanded the fortified area. While the goben was a consistent element of Gallic settlements and we translate the word as “blacksmith,” there were many different kinds of metalworking skills used to create the breadth of objects we are fortunate to have recovered. It’s likely that settlements would have specialized into particular metalcrafts depending on their resources at hand and their specific artisans.

A dūnon was a fortified settlement, typically located on a hill or other elevated position. In the early La Tène period, these would have enclosed only the most essential elements of the settlement, generally a workshop and sanctuary, but beginning in the second century BCE, the fortified portion of settlements expanded to include much of the residential areas as well. These defensible towns were the oppida described by Julius Caesar in his Gallic Wars. Archaeologists use the Latin word “oppidum” interchangeably with the Spanish “castro” to refer broadly to walled settlements throughout Iron Age Europe.

Encircling the dūnon was an uninterrupted wall with a single pincer gate entering the settlement. These mura gallica, as Caesar termed them, were constructed of wood beams interlaid between rows of stone, providing a defense against both siege engines and fire. The gate was more ornate than the surrounding wall, serving as the threshold between the community and the external world. It was designed to resist invading forces by forcing them to approach through a kind of gauntlet that would have been vulnerable to archers and spearmen positioned safely behind the wall.

In northern Burgundy, a Celtic settlement dating back to the Late Bronze Age contains the site of the Vix complex. The palace, as it has sometimes been described, is composed of six large buildings oriented to the east that show signs of both domestic and feasting purposes. Most significant, though, is the nearby burial mound known as the Vix grave.

The grave dates back to around 500 BCE and contained the remains of a woman along with many ornate pieces of jewelry. She was buried in a chariot along with many grave goods, a funerary custom practiced by several Gallic tribes. Her demonstrably high status has led many to refer to her as the Lady of Vix, though her historical identity remains a mystery. It is possible she was a priestess or member of an elite merchant family as the highest social group at this time seems to have been based on trade.

The grave goods include a variety of artifacts that help us understand the breadth of trade in the period. An enormous bronze krater, a vessel for mixing wine, is one of the most famous finds from the site. Along with other goods from across the Mediterranean, it provides evidence both for significant wealth and a developed network of trade and exchange.

In 1984, a zinc sheet was discovered in Bern, Switzerland, inscribed with a dedication to Dobnoredus Gobannus, or world-traveling Gobannus, the Gallic god of smithcraft. The inscription was made in Greek letters, which suggests that Roman influence was not yet very strong in the area. Unfortunately, since it was discovered by a local workman who died soon after, the details of the find are lost to us. Though we cannot reliably date the inscription, it was likely made during the early Roman period.

The zinc which composes the tablet originally led scholars to believe the piece a forgery as zinc was not produced in the region before the Early Modern period. However, the metal sheet is composed of a different kind of zinc than that which we have today. Rather than having been found naturally or created specifically, it is composed of a lead-iron alloy with other trace components. Such a metal is a byproduct of smelting that tended to accumulate on the sides of smithing furnaces, what the Greek geographer Strabo termed “fake silver.” Though it was typically discarded as waste, the metal would have had special significance to Gallic metalsmiths, who seem to have collected it and dedicated it to their god.

The Coligny calendar is a Gallic lunar calendar found in the town of Coligny in central Eastern France. Though the bronze tablets date to the second century CE, it is likely a copy of an earlier calendar with various dates proposed reaching back to the second century BCE. The inscription details the days of each Gallic month, recording what seem to be festival days along with ill-omened days, across a five-year period. Many marks on the calendar have unknown significance.

The first month of the Gallic year is listed as Samonios which shares the same root as the Old Irish word for summer, “sam.” Similarly, the half-way month of the Gallic year is Giamonios, very similar to “gam,” the Old Irish word for winter. Although Old Irish dates to the early Medieval period, scholars have taken this evidence to support the argument for a wide Celtic presence across the continent and the British Isles throughout the Iron Age. This shared language is the academic meaning of “Celtic,” a separate term from the various peoples who spoke Celtic and the wide variety of cultural practices we see across Iron Age Europe.

In 387 BCE, an army of Senones, a Gallic tribe, under the command of their chieftain Brennus, sacked Rome in what is remembered as the first instance of Rome falling to outsiders. The Senones had been pressing into northern Italy in search of additional settlement land, feeling the pressures of expansion and population growth. At peace talks with Rome, a Roman ambassador killed one of the Gallic chieftains, an act that betrayed the common practice of treating ambassadors as neutral. When Rome chose to not punish the offender, the Gauls were greatly offended and decided to attack Rome. After winning the Battle of Allia about ten miles north of Rome, they marched on the city, burning buildings and indiscriminately killing its inhabitants.

The Romans retreated to the Capitoline Hill, the most defensible position of the city, and the Gauls settled into a siege. At one point, they attempted to climb up the hill under the cover of night, but the geese of Juno sounded the alarm, saving the Romans from certain defeat. The siege lasted seven months, until the Gauls and Romans finally came to the negotiating table, the Romans due to famine, and the Gauls due either to sickness or threats to their homeland. The Gauls demanded 1,000 pounds of gold to leave the city, and Livy claims that Brennus cheated by placing his sword on the weights. In response to Roman protests, he exclaimed, “Vae Victis!” commonly translated as “Woe to the vanquished.” The Roman humiliation of the sack, siege, and ransom would live in infamous memory for centuries and engender a deep hatred of the Gauls among the Roman people.

In Gallic tribes, druids served the role of priest, lorekeeper, educator, and judge. They would have overseen ritual and been a source of guidance for decision-making through their skill in divination. For any instances of civic dispute, the druids would have heard the disagreement and offered judgment. They seem to have also been the teachers of the tribe, educating their members in science, religion, and tradition. A key characteristic of the druids’ practice was a focus on memorization over written records, leading to our very limited examples of written material in the Gaulish language.

Across tribes, druids served as a kind of council for inter-tribal decisions. We know from Caesar that the druids met annually in a central location to decide larger disputes, and he reports that their decisions held across tribes, suggesting they were the highest level of authority in Gallic society. They did not participate in battle, but Diodorus Siculus reports that they could intervene on a battlefield for the purpose of peace, their very presence a force of neutrality.

Our Roman sources, from which we get most of our information about druids, variously reported a Gallic practice of ritual execution which the druids would have overseen. This seems to have been partially related to punishment for some crime, but in some cases, ritual sacrifice of an innocent victim seems to have taken place, particularly in cases of communal danger. It is difficult to determine the frequency of the practice, as the Romans had ample reason to paint the Gauls as inhumane. Archaeological evidence for ritual murder has been found throughout Celtic Europe though it is rare, suggesting the practice existed only in specific ritual cases rather than as a norm.

The Gaisatai were a group of Gallic warriors mentioned by the Roman historians and active during the third century BCE. These men were known for their massed charge into battle, a tactic designed to overwhelm and scatter the enemy due to the panic caused both by the rush of the men and the cacophony of battle cries and trumpets. Though Polybius describes them as being naked, most evidence suggests that professional Gallic warriors would have been outfitted with a helmet and cuirass. It is possible, however, that the Gaisatai went into battle bare-chested as part of their strategy to overwhelm.

Gaisatai literally means “those with spears,” and thus likely supports the common theory that the Gaisatai were bands of Gallic mercenaries who hired themselves out to other Gallic tribes, typically in altercations with Rome. Like most Gallic warriors, they carried a long spear, an oblong shield, and a heavy longsword for close combat. In 225 BCE at the Battle of Telamon, the Gaisatai and other Gallic forces stood firm against heavy Roman infantry but eventually fell to Rome’s superior cavalry. The Gaisatai were slaughtered or captured, their leader Aneroëstes and several followers committed suicide, and Rome went on to settle the formerly Celtic lands of Northern Italy.
